stem: **Why the Sun shines.** In the core of the Sun, at about $10^7$ K, a chain of reactions effectively fuses four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus, releasing about 26.7 MeV each time. Helium-4 has a binding energy of about 7.07 MeV per nucleon.

parts.stem: Such high temperatures are needed because
options: the nuclei must overcome their electrostatic repulsion
parts.model_answer: **(B)** Only very fast nuclei get close enough for the nuclear force to act.

parts.stem: The mass converted into energy in each such reaction is about
The total binding energy of a helium-4 nucleus is about
The most tightly bound nuclei, with the highest binding energy per nucleon, are near
parts.model_answer: **(C)** The curve peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56.

hint: Mass converted = energy ÷ 931.5 MeV per u. Total binding energy = BE per nucleon × number of nucleons.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 4 one-line answers: option letter + reason · 4 minutes*

**(i) (B)** <mark>the nuclei must overcome their electrostatic repulsion</mark>; only very fast nuclei get close enough for the nuclear force to act.

**(ii) (A) 0.0287 u.**

$$\Delta m=\frac{26.7}{931.5}\approx0.0287\ \text{u}$$

**(iii) (C) 28.3 MeV.** $4\times7.07=28.3$ MeV.

**(iv) (C) iron-56.** The BE/A curve peaks at about 8.75 MeV near $A=56$.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the option letter for each part
- a one-line reason or the working for every numerical part
:::

**Marks are lost for:** "hydrogen must be ionised"; 7.07 MeV as the total in (iii).

label: PYQ-style
stem: Show that the density of nuclear matter is the same for all nuclei.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 3–4 lines · 3 minutes*

Mass of a nucleus of mass number A: $M\approx Am$ ($m$ = mass of one nucleon).

Radius $R=R_0A^{1/3}$, so the volume is

$$V=\tfrac43\pi R_0^3A$$

$$\rho=\frac{M}{V}=\frac{Am}{\tfrac43\pi R_0^3A}$$

$$\boxed{\rho=\frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}}$$

<mark>A cancels, so ρ is the same for all nuclei</mark> (about $2.3\times10^{17}$ kg m⁻³).

:::tip Your answer must contain
- $R=R_0A^{1/3}$
- A cancelling in the final step
:::

**Marks are lost for:** stating the result without $R\propto A^{1/3}$.

scheme.step: Mass of a nucleus $\approx Am$; radius $R=R_0A^{1/3}$, so volume $=\tfrac43\pi R_0^3A$.
$\rho=\dfrac{Am}{\frac43\pi R_0^3A}=\dfrac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3}$: independent of $A$ (about $2.3\times10^{17}$ kg m⁻³).

hint: Use R = R₀A^(1/3), so the volume is proportional to A. So is the mass.

label: PYQ-style
stem: Find the binding energy and the binding energy per nucleon of $^4_2$He. Mass of He-4 nucleus $=4.001506$ u, $m_p=1.007276$ u, $m_n=1.008665$ u, 1 u $=931.5$ MeV.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about 6 lines · 5 minutes* **Given:** $M_\text{He}=4.001506$ u, $m_p=1.007276$ u, $m_n=1.008665$ u, 1 u = 931.5 MeV
**To find:** $E_b$ and $E_b/A$ **Mass defect:** $$\Delta M=2m_p+2m_n-M_\text{He}$$ $$\Delta M=2.014552+2.017330$$ $$\qquad-4.001506$$ $$\Delta M=0.030376\ \text{u}$$ **Binding energy:** $$E_b=\Delta M\times931.5=0.030376\times931.5$$ $$\boxed{E_b\approx28.3\ \text{MeV}}$$ **Per nucleon** ($A=4$): $$\boxed{\frac{E_b}{A}\approx7.07\ \text{MeV per nucleon}}$$ He-4 is unusually tightly bound for a light nucleus (a peak on the BE/A curve). :::tip Your answer must contain - the mass defect line with 2 protons and 2 neutrons - × 931.5 MeV/u - both answers with units ::: **Marks are lost for:** rounding the masses before subtracting (the defect is a small difference); dividing by 2 instead of 4.
hint: Mass defect = (mass of 2 protons + 2 neutrons) − mass of the nucleus. Then multiply by 931.5 MeV per u.

stem: Draw the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number. Use it to explain the release of energy in (i) fission and (ii) fusion.
model_answer: *How much to write: a labelled graph and 2 points · 6 minutes* **Graph:** BE per nucleon rises steeply for light nuclei, stays near 8 MeV for $30peaks at about 8.75 MeV near A = 56, and falls gently to about 7.6 MeV for uranium. **(i) Fission:** a heavy nucleus ($A\approx235$, about 7.6 MeV per nucleon) splits into two middle nuclei (about 8.5 MeV per nucleon). Total binding energy goes up; the difference is released (about 200 MeV per fission). **(ii) Fusion:** two light nuclei join into one with a higher BE per nucleon (moving up the steep part towards the peak); again the gain in binding energy is released. :::tip Your answer must contain - a graph with axes labelled and the peak at A ≈ 56 - for both: products have higher BE per nucleon, so energy is released ::: **Marks are lost for:** saying energy is released because binding energy falls; no axis labels.

scheme.step: Graph: rises steeply for light nuclei, about 8 MeV over $30<A<170$, peak ≈ 8.75 MeV near $A=56$, gently falls to ≈ 7.6 MeV for uranium.
(i) A heavy nucleus ($A\approx235$) splits into two medium nuclei with higher BE per nucleon; total binding energy increases and the difference is released.
(ii) Two light nuclei fuse into one with higher BE per nucleon (towards the peak), again releasing the difference.

hint: Sketch BE/A against A: steep rise, flat top near 8 MeV, peak at A ≈ 56. Moving towards the peak releases energy.
